learning-curve.name: Learning curve
learning-curve.definition: A plot of model performance against a stated measure of learning progress, such as update count or training-set size.
learning-curve.explanation: This chapter records ordinary MSE on the complete training and validation partitions after each epoch. The optimized objective may include L2, but the two displayed curves omit that penalty so they share a definition. Curves help distinguish instability from possible overfitting, but their interpretation also depends on sample noise, distribution and measurement interval. Other learning curves vary training-set size; always inspect the horizontal axis.

minibatch.name: Minibatch
minibatch.definition: A subset of training examples used to estimate one optimizer step.
minibatch.explanation: A minibatch is one subset whose mean gradient produces an optimizer step. This lab shuffles only training rows with supplied deterministic RNG state, then uses chunks of the requested size. Each chunk averages by its actual length, including a short final chunk. An epoch visits the complete training set and can contain several steps, so comparisons should state both epochs and update counts.

regularization.name: Regularization
regularization.definition: A modification intended to favor models that transfer better to unseen data.
regularization.explanation: The lab adds lambda times weight squared to each batch-mean training objective. Its derivative is2lambda times the old weight; bias is unpenalized. Data-loss curves omit the penalty so training and validation share a metric definition. Lambda is selected using validation evidence. Regularization cannot repair unavailable features, leakage or a distribution mismatch.

generalization.name: Generalization
generalization.definition: Useful performance on relevant examples that were not used to fit the model.
generalization.explanation: Training minimizes an empirical objective on observed samples, but the real aim is usually performance on future data from the intended setting. A validation or test split provides an estimate of this transfer under assumptions about how the samples were collected. Generalization is not simply low training loss, and a synthetic held-out result does not establish real-world reliability. Model capacity, data quantity, noise, regularization, and distribution shift all affect the gap.
